identification.summary: Amaranth-Dragon is a name used by Check Point Research for a previously undocumented activity cluster that it says shares links to the China-affiliated APT41 ecosystem [S1]. Check Point reported campaigns in 2025 against government and law enforcement organizations in Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Indonesia, Singapore and the Philippines, typically focused on one or two countries at a time [S1][S4]. The cluster rapidly weaponized WinRAR CVE-2025-8088, with exploitation reported from 18 August 2025, four days after a working exploit became public [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Check Point reports tracking the activity since March 2025 [S5].
identification.notes: The name is Check Point's; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found in the sources gathered. Check Point describes the link to APT41 as overlap in tooling and operational patterns, not a confirmed merger of clusters [S1][S4]. Keep Amaranth-Dragon distinct from APT41 (Microsoft: Brass Typhoon) when citing.

attribution.confidence: Check Point Research assesses the actor is closely linked to, or part of, the APT41 ecosystem, based on shared tooling and operational patterns [S1][S4]. No government attribution to a specific PRC organization was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Check Point cites similarities between the custom Amaranth Loader and tools associated with APT41 (DodgeBox, Dustpan, Dusttrap) [S4]. Analysis of file compilation times and campaign timelines suggests the operators work in UTC+8 (China Standard Time) [S4].

objectives: Espionage against ASEAN-region government and law enforcement organizations, based on the victim set and event-themed lures reported by Check Point [S1][S5]. Specific collection requirements are not stated in the sources gathered.

targeting.notes: Campaigns were each restricted to one or two countries [S1]. One secondary report adds further Southeast Asian states (Brunei, Malaysia, Myanmar, Timor-Leste, Vietnam); this is not confirmed by the Check Point summary and should be treated as unverified [S7]. Lures were themed around geopolitical or local events [S5].

capabilities.summary: Early campaigns used ZIP archives containing LNK and BAT files that decrypt and run the Amaranth Loader via DLL side-loading . Later campaigns exploited WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 (path traversal) to place a script in the Startup folder and create a Registry Run key, launching the loader [S5]. The loader is a custom 64-bit DLL that fetches an AES key and decrypts a payload in memory; the final payload was usually the open-source Havoc C2 framework [S4]. TGAmaranth RAT, a Telegram-bot-controlled RAT with anti-debugging and anti-AV features, was used in some intrusions [S5]. C2 servers sat behind Cloudflare and answered only to IP addresses from the targeted country, returning HTTP 403 otherwise [S4].

campaigns.name: Early ZIP/LNK/BAT campaigns
campaigns.summary: Earliest activity Check Point tracks; ZIP files with LNK and BAT files launched the Amaranth Loader by DLL side-loading.

campaigns.name: CVE-2025-8088 exploitation begins
campaigns.summary: Reported start of WinRAR exploitation, four days after the first working public exploit; script dropped in Startup folder plus Run key to launch the loader and Havoc.

campaigns.name: TGAmaranth RAT campaign (Indonesia)
campaigns.summary: Telegram-based RAT with hard-coded bot first seen in an early September campaign against Indonesia, delivered via a password-protected RAR from a cloud storage service.

campaigns.name: Philippines Coast Guard-themed campaign
campaigns.summary: Late October campaign with Philippines Coast Guard lures and a similar attack sequence.

campaigns.name: Check Point publication
campaigns.summary: Check Point Research publicly documents the cluster and its campaigns.

diamond.adversary: Unnamed cluster assessed as linked to the APT41 ecosystem; operators apparently work in UTC+8 [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Amaranth Loader (DLL side-loading), Havoc C2, TGAmaranth RAT, WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 exploit, LNK/BAT droppers [S5].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 behind Cloudflare with country-level geofencing (HTTP 403 for non-target IPs); malicious archives hosted on cloud services; Telegram bot C2 for the RAT [S5].
diamond.victim: Government and law enforcement organizations in six ASEAN countries [S1][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Lures tied to real geopolitical and local events suggest regional political and security intelligence interest; sponsor intent is not stated in sources [S5].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with unpatched WinRAR (fixed in 7.13) and users who open archive attachments; cloud-hosted payload delivery [S5].

gaps: Primary Check Point Research report (research.checkpoint.com) could not be opened; details rest on Check Point's blog summary as returned by search and on secondary coverage.

A secondary aggregator gave specific 2025 campaign dates (19 March Cambodia, 28 April Cambodia, 3 July Thailand/Laos, 18 August Indonesia) that were not verified against the primary report and are not used as fact here.
One aggregator said the October Philippines campaign did not use CVE-2025-8088; unverified.
No government attribution, sponsor organization, Microsoft name or MITRE ID found.
Extent of overlap with APT41 (Brass Typhoon) infrastructure or personnel is unknown; the link is assessed from tooling similarity.
Victim names, data stolen and any post-Havoc activity are not public in the sources gathered.
No activity after the late-2025 campaigns is documented in the sources gathered.

Two secondary news sources (The Hacker News and Infosecurity Magazine) were dropped during fact-checking because their URLs could not be confirmed in search results; claims resting only on them were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is end-user Windows workstations in partner-nation government and law-enforcement networks, and the cloud file-hosting services used to deliver archives. STEP 2: The actor operationalizes newly disclosed archive-tool vulnerabilities within days and geofences C2, so researchers and defenders outside the target country may see nothing [S5]. STEP 3: The template is an event-themed lure, a RAR/ZIP archive, Startup-folder or Run-key persistence, a side-loaded loader, then Havoc or a Telegram RAT [S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against ASEAN government and law-enforcement targets, one or two countries per campaign. MDCOA is retargeting to defense or maritime organizations, or US/coalition personnel working with partners, using lures on regional security events (the Philippines Coast Guard lure is an indicator of maritime interest) . Candidate indicators: WinRAR versions below 7.13 on endpoints, scripts written to Startup folders from archives, new Run keys, side-loaded DLLs, Telegram API traffic from servers, and unexpected Havoc beacons [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: partner-nation ASEAN networks are the observed victims, so shared-indicator exchange with partners matters; geofenced C2 means local telemetry from the victim country is required to see the infrastructure . (2) Authorities: monitoring or hunting on partner networks requires partner consent and the appropriate agreements; US-network action follows normal DODIN and DCO authorities. (3) Mission assurance: enforce WinRAR 7.13 or later and restrict archive handling on mission systems, since exploitation began days after exploit release [S5]. (4) Coordination: coordinate with allied cyber centers and the vendor (Check Point) for indicators, and with DC3 where contractors are exposed.

provenance.importedSummary: Amaranth-Dragon is a previously untracked threat actor assessed to be closely linked to the China-affiliated APT 41 ecosystem, exhibiting similar tooling and operational patterns. The group demonstrated technical maturity by rapidly operationalizing CVE-2025-8088, a vulnerability in WinRAR, shortly after its public disclosure. Check Point Research has identified multiple campaigns targeting Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Indonesia, Singapore, and the Philippines, with operations typically focused on one or two countries at a time. The overlaps in technical and operational indicators strongly suggest that Amaranth-Dragon is either affiliated with or part of the broader APT-41 ecosystem.
